title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Morality in the City

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the strangest, richest novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1865, and it remains one of his most ambitious — and most unsettling.
It opens with a corpse pulled from the Thames, and it never quite lets you forget that money and death are its twin obsessions.
Today we are beginning at the beginning — with the question the novel poses on almost every page: what does wealth do to people, and what does poverty do to them?
I am joined by three exceptional readers of this novel, each bringing a very different set of tools to the text.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — the institutions, the mechanisms, the damage done.
He has a gift for finding the politics hidden in what looks like comedy, and Our Mutual Friend rewards that gift enormously.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions actually were — the workhouses, the courts, the river trade.
He has a dry wit and an even drier command of historical fact, which makes him invaluable when Dickens is being slippery about the real world.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has been reading this novel since she was a teenager and has never quite stopped.
She reads for the experience — the music of the sentences, the moments that make you put the book down and stare at the ceiling.
Let's begin with the novel's great theme — money and morality — and with a passage that gets at it in the most unexpected way: through a very badly fitting suit.
Thank you — and I want to start with something that looks like pure Dickensian farce but is actually doing something quite serious.
We have Sloppy — this large, ungainly young man who has been given a new black suit by the benevolent Mrs Boffin.
The tailor has been instructed — with great seriousness, by Rokesmith himself — to conceal Sloppy's buttons.
The system is deployed in full: the cunning of tailoring art, personal directions, the utmost resources of the craft.
And it fails completely — because Sloppy's body simply refuses to be dressed up as something it is not.
Listen to what Dickens does with that failure:
"he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
A hundred eyes of bright metal — it's comic, yes, but it is also the body of the poor exposing itself despite every institutional effort to cover it up.
The novel keeps doing this: the charity dresses the poor in respectability, and the poor keep bursting out of it.
That image rewards a bit of historical grounding, I think.
The black suit of mourning had a very specific class valence in mid-Victorian England — it was the costume of respectability, of people who observed the proper rituals of grief and social station.
Dressing Sloppy in it is an act of social translation — the Boffins are trying to move him up, or at least make him legible to the middle-class world they now inhabit.
But what Daniel is pointing at is precisely the limit of that project — the body won't cooperate.
And Dickens, to his credit, makes that funny rather than mournful — which is its own kind of commentary on the whole charade.
What I love about that passage is the sheer accumulation of the prose — it keeps going, it keeps finding more things wrong with the suit.
The trousers have hitched up at the ankles and bagged at the knees, the sleeves have migrated to his elbows, the coat has a yawning gulf at the waistband.
And then there is that hatband — "terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted."
The imagination shrunk discomfited — Dickens is writing about a hat.
But that absurdly elevated language — imagination, reason, discomfited — is the joke and the affection at the same time.
He adores Sloppy, and the comedy is never cruel.
That distinction matters enormously — because the novel also contains cruelty dressed up as comedy, and you have to know the difference.
What saves the Sloppy scene is that the system is the joke, not Sloppy himself.
And that becomes the template for the novel's deepest moral argument — which I think crystallises most powerfully when we come to Lizzie Hexam.
Here is a woman at the very bottom of the social order, in love with a man — Eugene Wrayburn — who represents everything that system values and she does not.
And she says something that I find genuinely startling in its selflessness — and also in what it reveals about the system that has shaped her.
"I love him so much, and so dearly, that when I sometimes think my life may be but a weary one, I am proud of it and glad of it.
I am proud and glad to suffer something for him, even though it is of no service to him, and he will never know of it or care for it."
The poor woman has so thoroughly internalised her own expendability that she calls it pride.
That is what the system produces — and Dickens is at least honest enough to let us see it.
I want to sit with that for a moment, because I think Daniel is right — but I also think there is another layer.
The novel is also tracking what happens when that invisible sacrifice finally forces the hand of the powerful — when Eugene nearly dies and can no longer pretend the gulf between them doesn't matter.
And there is a moment, when he is lying broken in bed, that Dickens gives him an extraordinary instruction to Mortimer:
"I trust to you that the perpetrator is never brought to justice."
He is asking Mortimer to bury the law — to protect Lizzie's name from the publicity of a trial.
Which is, of course, a wealthy man's privilege — the ability to decide that the law simply will not apply in this case.
Whether that is redemption or just power wearing a kinder face — the novel, to its credit, does not entirely resolve that question.
And then there is the sheer gothic horror of what the money has already done — before any of this moral reckoning even begins.
The passage where John Harmon — or the man we come to know as Rokesmith — discovers what has happened to his own supposed corpse is extraordinary.
He goes out at night, finds a placard in Whitehall — describing himself, John Harmon, as found dead and mutilated in the river.
He rushes to see the body.
And then comes the realisation — and I want to read this exactly as Dickens wrote it, because the rhythm carries the horror:
"I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me,
and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide, when the stream ran deep and strong."
The same dark place, the same dark tide.
The repetition is devastating — because money has made killer and intended victim interchangeable.
The river doesn't distinguish.
That image of the river — indifferent, equalising, dark — is one we'll be returning to throughout this episode.
For now, I want to thank Daniel, James, and Caroline for a genuinely electric opening.
We have established the stakes: class, money, the bodies that the system cannot quite dress up, and the river that takes everything.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the great dust heaps and what Dickens makes of the fortune built on rubbish.

segments.title: The Dust Heap's Dirty Secret: Class, Wealth, and Boffin's Moral Reckoning

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart, piece by piece, to see what's really inside.
Today's segment takes us to the heart of the novel's obsession with money — who has it, who wants it, and what it does to everyone it touches.
We're calling it 'The Dust Heap's Dirty Secret: Class, Wealth, and Boffin's Moral Reckoning.'
Joining me today are three people I trust absolutely to do justice to this extraordinary novel.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as a record of class power — its mechanisms, its contradictions, its victims.
He's particularly sharp on what Dickens knew that Dickens perhaps didn't quite admit to himself.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the institutions alive — the workhouse, the courts, the debt laws — as they actually operated.
He has a dry wit that I find extremely useful when we're discussing the upper classes.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and reader who has lived with this novel since her teens and brings a reader's instinct — for the music, the feeling, the moments that make you stop.
Caroline, Daniel, James — welcome, all three.
Let's begin with Boffin himself — a man who inherits a dust heap fortune and becomes, almost overnight, the target of every species of human greed.
Daniel, I want to start with you — because Dickens does something quite startling in how he frames Boffin's fundamental character.
Yes, and the passage that establishes this is one of the most quietly radical moments in the novel.
Dickens is describing the Boffins in a moment of unusual candour — calling them, flat out, 'ignorant and unpolished.'
But then he pivots immediately — and this is what matters — to their moral life.
He says they have been guided, all their lives, by — and I want to read this carefully —
'a religious sense of duty and desire to do right.'
Now, Dickens is making a claim here that would have stung his readers: that education and polish are entirely beside the point when it comes to moral worth.
The class system told you that refinement was virtue. Dickens says: look at the Boffins.
And then he ends with a line that operates almost like a theorem — a law of moral physics.
'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
That 'never' is doing an enormous amount of work. It's almost defiant.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is how Dickens earns that final aphorism.
He doesn't just announce it. He builds the ground for it — through old Harmon, who squeezed the Boffins for every bit of labour and paid them as little as he could.
And yet even that 'hard wrathful and sordid nature' — Dickens's own words — 'knew their moral straightness and respected it.'
What Dickens is describing is goodness as a kind of gravitational force. It bends even cruelty toward it.
I find that genuinely moving — and also more complicated than it looks.
Because the novel then proceeds to test that thesis very rigorously indeed.
The test arrives very quickly, and it takes the form of the post.
The moment Boffin's fortune becomes public knowledge, he is deluged — and the word isn't too strong — with requests for money.
What Dickens anatomises here is the entire machinery of Victorian charity — or rather, the parasitic relationship that called itself charity.
The Secretary opens these letters, and Dickens gives us this extraordinary satirical inventory.
'Fifty-seven churches to be erected with half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings, seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence.'
The comedy is in the absurd specificity — but beneath it is a real and accurate picture of how Victorian philanthropy operated.
Newly wealthy men were systematically targeted by charitable organisations that were, in many cases, essentially patronage networks for the upper classes.
And then there is the duke's letter, which is the gem of the passage.
The duke's letter — yes, I was hoping you'd get there. Because it's one of Dickens's sharpest comic set-pieces, isn't it.
James, would you read us the punchline?
With pleasure. The letter begins solemnly: it is a 'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
The Duke of Linseed writes, in his own hand apparently, to assure Nicodemus Boffin Esquire of his deep personal interest in the Family Party Fund.
And then comes the postscript:
'P.S. The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas.'
And Dickens adds, calmly: this letter has been 'lithographed by the hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address.'
A mass-produced personal letter from a duke. The irony is surgical.
What I want to underline is the class architecture of all this.
It takes 'two noble Earls and a Viscount, combined' — again, Dickens's exact phrase — to solicit Boffin for another scheme.
The aristocracy is not performing charity. It is laundering social capital through the mechanism of charity.
Boffin's gold — earned from dust, from the labour of sorting and sifting — is the real substance here.
The nobility contributes their names. Boffin contributes actual money. That is the transaction.
And then Dickens turns, and the comedy drops away entirely — into something much darker.
Because after the corporate beggars — the dukes and earls — come the individual beggars.
And Dickens does something very interesting with their letters.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
There it is — the satirist's scalpel, and the humanitarian's grief, in a single sentence.
These are people ground down to scraps of paper, desperately performing the forms of respectable correspondence.
The daughters of generals who cannot spell. The wives and husbands writing in secret from each other. The man with the violin and the clock.
Dickens is pitiless about their pretensions — and utterly compassionate about their need.
The beggars of punctual business-habits are the ones that stop me every time.
These are people who announce that they will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday.
And Dickens records that if the postal order arrives late, 'it need not be sent, as they will then be cold in death.'
It's blackly funny — and it isn't.
Because in the 1860s, suicide as a consequence of debt and destitution was not a rhetorical flourish.
It was an outcome the Victorian state had engineered with some efficiency, and seemed entirely disinclined to prevent.
Which brings us directly to Betty Higden — and the passage that I think is the most disturbing in the entire novel.
Dickens sends her along the Thames, dying, fleeing the workhouse — fleeing, specifically, the Poor Law and the Relieving Officer.
And he imagines the river itself whispering to her.
'Come to me, come to me! When the cruel shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me!'
'I am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I am not held in estimation according as I shirk it.'
'My breast is softer than the pauper-nurse's; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the pauper-wards.'
The river offers Betty Higden what the state refuses her: a death without shame.
Dickens has cast the Thames as a better Poor Law than the one Parliament legislated.
That is not a sentimental gesture. That is an indictment.
I read that passage differently, though not in opposition to Daniel.
What undoes me is the moment just before the river speaks — that image of the young river, 'dimpled like a young child, playfully gliding away among the trees.'
The river begins innocent. And then it becomes the only tenderness available to this old woman.
Dickens is careful to say she didn't quite consciously formulate these thoughts.
But she 'heard the tender river whispering' — and that word 'tender' is doing everything.
The state gives her fear. The river gives her tenderness. The comparison is moral catastrophe for the Victorian Poor Law.
Let me add something from the legal end of the novel, because Dickens is not only indicting the Poor Law.
There's a passage involving Twemlow — gentle, bewildered Twemlow — that reads almost like a casebook on how debt law destroyed lives in the middle of the century.
He had 'given his name' for a friend — that is, co-signed a debt — and the friend died, leaving Twemlow to repay money he had never received.
Dickens puts it like this — and the precision of it is almost cruel:
'always to observe great economy, being in the enjoyment of a fixed income limited in extent, and that depending on the munificence of a certain nobleman'
'and had always pinched the full interest out of himself with punctual pinches.'
'Pinched the full interest out of himself with punctual pinches.' That phrase — the repetition of 'pinch' — is Dickens at his most physical.
You feel the economy in the body. You feel what years of living below your means actually does to a person.
And who now holds the debt? Riah — acting, as we know, as front-man for Fledgeby.
The novel is very precise about this architecture of exploitation: the money-lender, the aristocratic debtor, the shadow of 'the awful Snigsworth' looming in the background as notional security.
Dickens calls Snigsworth 'Security in the Mist.'
'Through which stalked the shadow of the awful Snigsworth, eyed afar off by money-lenders as Security in the Mist.'
The aristocracy is not in the room. It never is. But it is the collateral on which the whole system rests.
And Wegg's discovery of the will tells us something very similar about the original Harmon fortune.
The will is a revelation of how arbitrary inherited wealth actually is.

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
The entire fortune — everything that has set this novel in motion — goes to the Crown because one man had no friends and hated his family.
That is the moral logic of inheritance law. Pure accident. Pure spite.
And yet Dickens chooses Boffin as the recipient of what does remain — the Little Mound.
Not the polished characters. Not the legally correct heirs. The good, unpolished, morally straight Boffin.
So the novel holds two things in tension: the system is corrupt and arbitrary, AND individual virtue can still navigate it.
Whether that tension resolves satisfyingly or not — I think about that every time I read it.
And I think that is precisely the right place to pause — on that unresolved tension.
A system that is genuinely rotten, and individuals who somehow remain genuinely good within it.
Daniel, James, Caroline — thank you.
We'll be back shortly to dig into how Dickens constructs his villains — and whether they're quite as villainous as they first appear.

segments.title: Bella's Price: A Woman's Education in Love and Greed

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and without mercy.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most extraordinary arcs: Bella Wilfer's education in love and money.
Bella begins the novel as a self-declared mercenary — determined to marry for wealth — and ends it having chosen something harder and rarer.
But this transformation doesn't happen in a vacuum.
It happens because a man stages an elaborate deception to test her — and because the novel lets us watch her be tested without her knowledge.
To help us think through all of this, I'm joined by three brilliant readers of this novel.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who, I suspect, has some sharp things to say about a man who disguises himself as a poor clerk to assess a woman's moral worth.

Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he'll tell us what the institutions in this novel actually were, and what it meant, in Victorian England, to be the kind of person this novel's machinery grinds up.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence — she's the one who'll make us hear the sentences properly.
Let's begin with John Harmon's confession — the long retrospective in which he explains why he decided to stay dead.
Daniel, I want to start with you — because the logic of what Harmon does is, on its face, staggering.
It is staggering — and yet the novel asks us to accept it as a kind of romantic nobility.
Harmon arrives in England already cringing from what his inheritance represents.
Dickens gives us the exact texture of that cringe — listen to the accumulation here.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
Three-fold repetition — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — and the object of every fear is a woman or money, and usually both at once.
What I find fascinating — and troubling — is that Harmon's solution to the problem of mercenary marriage is surveillance.
He disguises himself as a common sailor, he plants himself in Bella's neighbourhood, he watches her.
The novel frames this as love — I'd call it an audit.
That word — audit — is very precise, and I think it's right.
But there's something else happening in that passage that I can't quite let go of.
Dickens gives us the plot in Harmon's own voice, this almost bureaucratic recitation — and then Harmon keeps interrupting himself to verify his own facts.
'I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right.'
It reads like a man trying to convince himself that the story he's telling — the story that excuses everything — is actually true.
There's enormous psychological subtlety in that tic.
Dickens may be more critical of Harmon than Harmon is of himself.
I want to come at this from a slightly different angle, because the historical context matters enormously here.
A woman in Bella's position — promised by her father's will to a man she's never met, entirely dependent on the Boffins' goodwill — had almost no legal standing whatsoever.
So Harmon frames his anxiety as moral timidity — Dickens is precise about that phrase.
He tells us that the deception arose from, and I'm quoting directly here,
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
Proving Bella.
She is a proposition to be tested, a hypothesis to be verified — while she remains entirely ignorant of the experiment being run on her life.
The law in 1865 would have said nothing wrong with this arrangement. That, I think, tells you everything.
James puts his finger on it — and there's a passage in chapter thirty-one that makes the bind even more explicit.
Dickens lays out what I think is the novel's most honest accounting of what Harmon's position actually is.
He's trapped between two versions of cowardice — buying Bella by accepting the inheritance, or punishing her by rejecting it.
But before that — and this is the sentence I keep coming back to — Dickens traces the deception back to its psychological origin.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
'Meant to be harmless.' That is doing a great deal of work.
The novel is quietly, devastatingly ironic — because of course it was not harmless.
It reshaped two lives and put at least one person — Bella — through an experience she never consented to and never fully understood.
And yet — and this is what I wrestle with every time I re-read it — Bella does change.
Genuinely, deeply, in ways that feel earned rather than imposed.
The question the novel keeps circling is whether the transformation justifies the method — and I don't think Dickens ever fully answers it.
What's interesting is that the deception starts as something imposed on Bella — and ends as something she half-chooses, by choosing Rokesmith without knowing who he is.
So in a strange way, she does pass the test — on her own terms.
I want to bring in a passage that sits alongside all of this — because Bella's story doesn't exist in isolation.
The novel surrounds her with another child — unnamed, ailing, trapped in a world of drink and degradation — and Lizzie Hexam describes that child with a precision that should make us uncomfortable.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
If she ever had a cradle.
That parenthesis is almost unbearable — the casual devastation of it.
Bella gets an education in value through a romantic plot. This child gets nothing — not even the presumption of a cradle.
That is the novel's structural argument, right there.
Bella's transformation is possible because she has a position — she's the designated heroine of a plot about inherited wealth.
The child Lizzie describes has no such position.
The father is 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober' — and the system that made him that way continues entirely undisturbed.
Dickens can redeem individuals — he does it brilliantly with Bella.
What the novel cannot quite bring itself to imagine is the redemption of the conditions that produce those unnamed ailing children.
And yet Dickens does something sharp with the institutions that claim to address those conditions.
There's a wonderful passage — comic but with real venom in it — where Boffin tears into the whole apparatus of Victorian philanthropy.
He's complaining about the titles in charity subscription books, and the outrage just keeps building.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses — what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
'Pretty well up to his neck.' The image is drowning — and it's drowning in bureaucratic self-congratulation.
That child with no cradle isn't being saved by any of these Patrons and Vice-Patronesses.
Boffin's rant is historically precise, and that's what gives it its real force.
Victorian charitable organisations were absolutely awash in honorific titles that cost nothing and did nothing.
A five-shilling subscription bought you a Patroness-ship and a listing in the annual report — and the annual report was largely the point.
Dickens puts this critique in Boffin's mouth — a man who actually has money and is actually confused by what's being asked of it.
There's a kind of innocent radicalism in Boffin's bafflement that Dickens couldn't have delivered through a more knowing character.
Boffin is one of those characters who reveals more than he intends to — or more than his author perhaps intended.
His bewilderment at the charity titles is the bewilderment of someone who still thinks money ought to correspond to something real.
And of course, in Dickens's world, the whole point of the novel is that it doesn't — and it never did.
Harmon's father made his fortune from dust and refuse.
The Patronesses with their five shillings are just a cleaner version of the same performance.
That feels like the right note to pause on — the idea that every performance of virtue in this novel is haunted by the question of what it actually costs.
Bella's education, Harmon's deception, Boffin's bewilderment — they all circle that same question.
We'll be back shortly to look at how the novel handles the moment when the deception finally unravels — and what it costs the people who've been living inside it.

segments.title: Dead Men Tell Tales: Harmon's Masquerade and the Plot's Hidden Machinery

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart stitch by stitch to find what's really inside.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside the novel's central machinery — the disguise, the dead man who isn't dead, and the hidden generosities that quietly drive the whole plot forward.
With me are three guests who between them cover just about every angle you could want.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power — he'll keep us honest about who benefits and who pays.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he brings the real institutions of Victorian England into focus so we can see what Dickens was actually describing.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens — she'll tell us what it feels like on the page, sentence by sentence.
Our starting point today is a question the novel plants early and answers very, very late: who is John Harmon, and what has he done with himself?
What I find endlessly striking about the Harmon plot is that it begins not with John Harmon at all, but with the Boffins — and specifically with their grief.
Mrs Boffin has inherited a fortune from a man who treated the boy she loved like a piece of unwanted property.
And her response to that fortune is — extraordinary.
She says, gradually toning down to what Dickens calls a motherly strain:
'Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.'
She wants to resurrect John Harmon — not the man, but the name, the idea of him — through an act of pure tenderness.
And of course, the reader who knows the plot's secret understands that John Harmon is not past all benefit of the money at all.
He is present, in disguise, watching this woman mourn him.
That irony is devastating, and Dickens uses it with real precision.
But I want to hold on to something in that passage that we might slide past too quickly.
The Boffins' goodness toward John Harmon didn't emerge from wealth or comfort.
It was forged in direct, physical conflict with the old man — with Old Harmon's cruelty.
Mr Boffin describes what it actually cost them to stand by that boy.

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard.'

'And once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn't thrown herself betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
That repetition — 'Dropped her' — is Dickens at his most controlled.
The comic register of the spinning bonnet collides with the stark violence of that final phrase.
The Boffins are not naive do-gooders — they have paid in blood for their decency.
Daniel is right about the cost, and it's worth adding a historical dimension here.
Old Harmon is a patriarch operating within a perfectly legal framework.
A father could disinherit a child, send him away, ignore his existence — the law provided almost no recourse.
What the Boffins did in standing out against the old man, as Boffin puts it, was entirely extra-legal.
They had no standing, no authority — just conscience and stubbornness.
And it's precisely this moral standing, rather than legal standing, that the novel ultimately honours.
When Harmon finally reveals himself and settles accounts with Wegg, the whole resolution rests not on inheritance law but on a private compact with Boffin — which is itself entirely voluntary.
The law, as it so often does in Dickens, is simply beside the point.
That compact is one of the great moments in the novel, and it comes out in a speech that I find almost overwhelming on re-reading.
Harmon is confronting Wegg, and he stops to explain exactly what the Boffins mean to him.
'I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin.'
That parenthetical — 'there are no words to satisfy me' — is where the prose breaks open.
Dickens doesn't usually let his language confess its own inadequacy.
But here it does — and it's precisely that admission that makes the gratitude feel real rather than rhetorical.
And then, immediately after that tenderness, Harmon grabs Wegg by the cravat.
'The wonder is,' Dickens writes, 'that I didn't try to twist your head off, and fling that out of window.'
The violence is not a contradiction of the gratitude — it is its expression.
When someone you owe everything to is threatened by a parasite, the correct response is fury.
Dickens understands that — and he lets Harmon understand it too.
I want to bring in a passage that sits at an angle to all of this — because not every strand of the novel resolves with Harmon's clarity.
While Harmon is securing his future with Boffin's blessing, Bradley Headstone is disintegrating.
Dickens gives us a portrait of a man destroyed from the inside, under Riderhood's vigilant eye.

'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
That accumulation — lines deepening, stare haggard, surface whitening, hair degenerating — is a sentence that enacts the process it describes.
Each clause adds another stage of ruin.
It is the novel's dark mirror to the Harmon plot — where Harmon's concealment ultimately restores, Bradley's self-enclosure merely consumes.
And then there's the rooftop.
The passage with Lizzie and Jenny Wren on Riah's housetop garden is — for me — one of the loveliest things in the entire novel.
It's tucked into a chapter that also involves Fledgeby's horrible scheming, which makes the contrast all the sharper.
Dickens describes what Riah has prepared for them:

'Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet — they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces; Jenny with the sharper; Lizzie with the more perplexed.'
That small distinction — Jenny's sharper face, Lizzie's more perplexed — does so much work in so few words.
We see the two women as individuals, not a pair, even as they share a single book.
And the chimneys at the end — bridling, fanning themselves, looking on in airy surprise — the whole city becomes a comic audience for this quiet, private moment of grace.
The rooftop is necessary precisely because the street is impossible for those two.
Lizzie is marked by her connection to the river, to the criminal underworld of retrieval; Jenny is visibly disabled, visibly poor.
They have to go up and out of the city to find a space the city hasn't already claimed.
Riah's carpet is an act of hospitality that the novel's official spaces — the parlours, the law courts, the drawing rooms — simply couldn't extend.

What strikes me, drawing these threads together, is that all of these moments — Mrs Boffin's adoption scheme, the Boffins' physical courage, Harmon's confession of debt, the rooftop garden — are all about goodness that operates outside sanctioned structures.
The plot's machinery turns on secrets and disguises, but its moral engine runs on these quiet, private acts.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's darker undercurrents — the river, the dust, the bodies that won't stay buried.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: Laughter and Cruelty: Dickens's Comic Mask in a Mercenary World

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and without mercy.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel obsessed with money, death, identity, and reinvention — but it is also wickedly, ferociously funny.
Today we are looking at Dickens's comic mask — how he uses laughter to expose greed, cruelty, and the strange mercy that lurks underneath both.
With me are three guests who know this novel intimately and think about it in very different ways.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who suspects Dickens was more radical than he himself knew.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell you exactly what the institutions in this novel actually were — and exactly how they failed the people inside them.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager and whose ear for Dickens's prose I find genuinely enviable.
Caroline, let's start with you — because the passage that opens this novel is one of the strangest comic moments I know in all of fiction.
It really is extraordinary, isn't it.
We are, what, two pages into the novel — the Thames is dark, there's a body in the water — and then Gaffer Hexam climbs back into the boat.
He washes his arms over the side of the boat — they are wet and dirty — and then he washes something else in the river too.
'He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—"for luck," he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket.'
That triple rhythm — chinked, blew, spat — it's almost incantatory.
Dickens gives us the ritual of luck — the superstition of a man who pulls the dead from the river for a living — and makes it grotesquely funny.
And yet there's something almost tender in it, too.
This is a man whose entire economy depends on the dead, and he still needs luck.
What strikes me is that the money is washed in the same river as the body.
Not metaphorically — literally.
The coin is baptised in the same water as the corpse it was taken from.
Dickens places that on the first page because the entire novel is an argument that money and death in this society are inseparable.
The comedy is real — that 'hoarsely said' is a masterstroke — but it doesn't soften the image.
It sharpens it.
And we should be clear about what Gaffer is doing, legally speaking.
Thames mudlarks and river-finders in the mid-nineteenth century occupied a genuine — if precarious — legal niche.
The coroner's inquest would reward a finder for bringing in a body, and the property found on the body was — in practice — often pocketed without much scrutiny.
So when Dickens writes Gaffer washing the coins in the river, he is describing something that thousands of people in London did to survive — and did legally enough.
The comedy lands partly because we recognise it as the utterly mundane logic of a specific economic arrangement.
That mundanity is exactly where Dickens finds his comedy later in the novel too — with Wegg and Venus.
There's a scene where Wegg lays out his scheme for blackmailing Boffin, and it is delivered with such pompous procedural solemnity that it reads like a parody of a board meeting.
Dickens gives Wegg this extraordinary habit of addressing Venus as 'my comrade, brother, and partner' — over and over — as if repetition could conjure legitimacy.
And then comes the plan, which he delivers with the gravity of a legal brief.
'He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, "Halves!"'
And then he goes on — and this is where it tips into something darker — to describe how Boffin should be kept in what he calls 'a state of abject moral bondage and slavery.'
The word 'slavery' is not casual.
Dickens puts it in the mouth of a fool — which doesn't make it funny exactly; it makes it appalling.
Wegg is a brilliant creation precisely because he is a small man who has entirely absorbed the logic of the large men who exploit him.
He doesn't want to dismantle the system of extraction — he wants to be on the right side of it for once.
His fantasy of 'Halves!' is just capitalism with a different beneficiary.

And notice that even in his greed he cannot help offering corrections — 'it might be more according to the rights of things to say Two-thirds; it might be more according to the rights of things to say Three-fourths.'
He is always open to correction, he says — which is to say he will take as much as he can get.
The procedural parody goes very deep, I think.
The language Wegg uses — 'conditional clause,' 'plan of action,' 'by way of peroration' — is the language of the solicitor's office and the counting house.
Dickens is showing us that the forms of legitimate commerce and the forms of blackmail are essentially the same — the same grammar, the same rituals.
The comedy is in the exposure of that resemblance.
Though I will say — speaking of the law — that Wegg's scheme, while idiotic, is not entirely without precedent in Victorian blackmail cases.
And of course the joke on Wegg is catastrophic and entirely earned — Caroline, you have that passage.
The unmasking of Wegg is one of the great comic coups in Dickens — and it hinges entirely on a hat.
Someone enters by the folding-doors while Wegg is in full flow — and Dickens sets it up with this perfectly timed sentence.
'Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.'
'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
'A face that was Sloppy's.' That full stop does all the work.
Sloppy — this lumbering, good-natured, newspaper-reading boy — has been playing the terrifying dustman all along.
The word 'persecutor' applied to Sloppy is the funniest word in the chapter.
What I love about that moment is the costume.
'Fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete' — Dickens is very precise about that.
The working man's costume is the disguise — which tells you something about how invisible working men are to someone like Wegg.
He couldn't recognise Sloppy because he never really looked at Sloppy to begin with.
Let's turn now to the novel's gentler comedy — because not all of Dickens's laughter is savage.
Caroline, you've brought two passages about joy — which in this novel feels almost radical.
Joy in Our Mutual Friend is always precarious — it has to be earned and it has to be sheltered.
There's a scene where Bella and John Rokesmith and her father R. Wilfer share a simple supper — in a counting house, surrounded by the hardware of commerce.
And Dickens reaches for a nursery rhyme to describe it.

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, "Somebody's been drinking my milk!"'
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
That 'even R. Wilfer' — the little flourish at the end — is pure tenderness.
R. Wilfer has had so little joy in his life that his inclusion in the superlative feels like a gift.
And the brass knobs of the safe staring like 'the eyes of some dull dragon' — even the comedy of that image — only makes the warmth more vivid by contrast.
What strikes me there is the location — the counting house.
The names Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles are not incidental — Veneering is the hollow social climber at the heart of the novel's satire of the nouveaux riches.
The feast of simple human happiness takes place inside the machinery of that world.
Dickens makes the comedy of that incongruity do real emotional work — it tells us something about where joy can be found, and where it cannot.
There's a tenderness in the Wilfer family that Dickens rarely extends to the wealthy characters without irony.
R. Wilfer is a diminished man — diminished by poverty, by his marriage, by his position — and the novel keeps giving him these small, luminous moments.
The hobgoblin simile is funny, but what it actually says is: these people have never had enough, and now, just for a moment, they do.
And then there's Bella's reconciliation with Boffin — which is the comedy of unmasking used for entirely opposite ends to the Wegg scene.
Bella kneels beside him and launches into this extraordinary speech — and Dickens marks it with the word 'Please,' repeated, like a child asking forgiveness.
'Please I beg your pardon, and I made a small mistake of a word when I took leave of you last.'
And then it builds — 'Please something more! Please I have found out something not yet mentioned.'
'Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
That accumulation of 'Please' — it shouldn't work, and yet it's devastating.
The comedy of the child's register against the gravity of the revelation — Dickens earns that entirely.
Boffin's performance of miserliness is, structurally, the most radical thing in the novel.
A wealthy man deliberately degrades himself in the eyes of his ward — and of the reader — in order to improve her character.
It is a form of love that involves sustained self-humiliation.
And when Bella says 'I don't believe you ever for one single minute were' — she is absolving him of the performance.
Which is funny — with 'exultant ringing laugh,' Dickens says — and also an act of moral recognition.
The detail of the baby being placed in John's arms first — before Bella kneels — is quietly important.
She hands off the child so that she can kneel unencumbered.
There is something both comic and ceremonial about that — 'John dear, you're a good nurse; will you please hold baby?'
Domestic practicality and moral theatre running in parallel.
What this conversation has made vivid for me is how Dickens uses comedy as a form of intelligence — not relief from the darkness, but a way of seeing it more clearly.
From Gaffer washing a dead man's money in the Thames, to Sloppy's face emerging from under a tied-up head, to Bella's 'Please' — the laughter is always doing serious work.
My thanks to Daniel, James, and Caroline — we'll be back in a moment.

segments.title: Transformation Across Time: How Character Shapes and Reshapes Victorian Society

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to find out what's really going on.

I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's most compelling preoccupations: the way character — moral character, formed over years — either holds firm or buckles under the pressures of wealth and society.
With me to explore that territory are three wonderful guests.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as precise anatomies of class power — and who has a gift for finding the radical nerve beneath the surface of even the most cheerful Dickens scene.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian whose knowledge of the institutions — the courts, the workhouses, the rivers of Victorian England — gives every passage a whole new dimension.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel who brings us back to what it actually feels like to encounter these pages — the comedy, the shock, the ache.
Let's begin with the Boffins — that hopelessly, gloriously Unfashionable pair who inherit a dust-heap fortune and somehow remain exactly themselves.
What I love about the Boffins is that Dickens plays the scene absolutely straight — and that's what makes it so funny and so moving at once.
Mrs Boffin has social ambitions — genuine ones, bless her — and for a moment you think Dickens might let her have them.
And then Mr Boffin opens his mouth, and out comes this perfectly artless declaration of contentment.
He says — and I keep coming back to this —
"Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!"
And Dickens immediately delivers the verdict: it was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations — and there they sit, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
That capital U on Unfashionable is doing so much work.
Fashion becomes an institution with its own laws — and the Boffins are constitutionally unable to comply.
The comedy is real, but I don't think we should let it soften the point Dickens is making.
The Boffins are marked from the start as people whose virtue is precisely what makes them unfit for the class they've stumbled into.
That's not incidental — that's the whole architecture of Dickens's argument about money and character.
And it goes deeper when you look at how old John Harmon actually saw them — and why he left them the money at all.
Dickens tells us that this man — bitter, misanthropic, what the novel calls the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail — had recognised their integrity and been enraged by it.
The exact phrase is extraordinary — Dickens writes that
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
Wealth cannot buy integrity — and the misanthrope knows it, resents it, and honours it anyway in his will.
That is a very specific claim about the limits of capital.
There's a legal dimension to that bequest that's worth pausing on.
Old Harmon writes their names down in his will as trustees — not beneficiaries, initially, but trustees — because the one thing his money cannot manufacture is trustworthiness.
The institution of testamentary trust was built precisely on this problem: how do you project control beyond death when you can't trust the living?
Harmon's solution is bitter and self-aware — he mistrusts all mankind, Dickens says, and especially those who resemble himself.
The Boffins are trustworthy precisely because they bear no resemblance to him whatsoever.
And then this fortune lands on them — and the question the novel poses is whether the money will finally do what the old man's contempt and raillery never could: corrupt them.
That's exactly the tension that makes re-reading this novel so unnerving — because Dickens will appear to answer that question in the most disturbing way before he relents.
But there's another character who never relents — Eugene Wrayburn — and whose relationship to duty and identity is comic on the surface and quietly devastating beneath it.
Eugene has this extraordinary speech where he explains how his father, M. R. F. — the Most Respected Father — pre-assigned a destiny to every child before they could even object.
The delivery is so dry, so perfectly timed — listen to this:
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one — three words, and a whole life of quiet failure.
And Eugene tells this story not with bitterness — he says he can't help it if his father amuses him.
That detachment is both his charm and his wound.
Eugene's comedy about M. R. F. is the novel's sharpest sketch of how class reproduces itself through the family as institution.
The eldest inherits the Family Embarrassments — note that Dickens allows Eugene to name the truth and then immediately retract it into polite euphemism.
The younger sons are pitched into professions without consultation — church, navy, bar — like pieces being placed on a board.
And every single one of them fails to fulfil the role assigned — the pillar is shaky, the circumnavigator hasn't circumnavigated, Eugene the barrister does essentially nothing.
The system generates its own dysfunction, and the gentleman class carries the wreckage with languid good humour.
But of course Eugene's story doesn't end in languid irony.
The novel tracks him to the river — and Bradley Headstone tracks him there too, with rather different intentions.
There's a passage of landscape description in this section that I find genuinely chilling — and it works because it looks like pure atmosphere while actually announcing what is about to happen.
Dickens writes that as the sun went down, the landscape was dyed red — and then:
"And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does."
That phrase — as we say — is doing something very strange.
It invokes a communal knowledge, a cultural idiom about guilt — and implicates the reader in the foreknowledge of the crime.
We know before it happens — and we are made to feel that we have always known.
And what Headstone does with that guilt — or rather what he refuses to do — is where Dickens is most merciless as a psychologist.
There's no remorse in Headstone — none — and Dickens is careful not to give us the comfort of a straightforward guilty conscience.
Instead, he describes something more corrosive — a torture that arises not from repentance but from obsessive repetition.
The passage reads:
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
More efficiently — that word is monstrous.
The mind doesn't seek atonement — it seeks to perfect the crime.
This is what happens when a character shaped entirely by repression and thwarted desire is finally unleashed — and finds that there is no relief on the other side.
It's psychologically modern in a way that still startles me, even on re-reading.
Dickens understands that the absence of remorse is not freedom — it's a different kind of prison.
And the word he uses is wearisome — "a state of mind more wearing and more wearisome than remorse."
Wearisome — not agonising, not sublime — wearisome.
The grinding dailiness of that word is perfectly calibrated to a character who was always, at his core, ground down by the machinery of his own ambitions.
And that contrast with the Boffins is worth naming explicitly.
The Boffins are shaped by a life of honest service — and when fortune finds them, they remain, fundamentally, themselves.
Headstone is shaped by violent aspiration and social shame — and when his passion is thwarted, he shatters.
The novel suggests — with uncomfortable firmness — that character formed in dignity is more durable than character formed in resentment.
Whether that's a consolation or a reproach to the social order that produces men like Headstone is a question Dickens leaves pointedly open.
A question the novel certainly doesn't resolve — and perhaps that's precisely where its power lies.

From the tender immovability of the Boffins, to the languid irony of Eugene Wrayburn, to the grinding psychological torment of Bradley Headstone — Dickens gives us character not as destiny but as something forged and tested, passage by passage.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's great watery backdrop — the Thames — and asking what it means that so much of life, and death, in this book happens at the river's edge.

segments.title: Closing: Redemption and Dust—What Dickens Left Unsettled

utterances.text: We've spent this episode in the muck and the money, the drawing rooms and the river.
Now, as we close, I want to ask all three of you: what does this novel actually leave us with?
Redemption, dust, unfinished business — or something harder to name?
Caroline, you've loved this book for decades. I'll start with you.
What I keep coming back to, honestly, is the image of Mrs Boffin kneeling at the fire.
Boffin tells this memory of young John Harmon at seven years old — alone, going off to a foreign school, coming in just to get warm.
And then Dickens gives us this, in Boffin's own voice:
That phrase —
It's the most naked cry of helplessness in the whole novel.
A good woman, a warm woman, and she cannot save this child. Not yet.
The novel is about whether that rescue, delayed by decades, can still mean something.
That scene is devastating precisely because it shows who is permitted to care and who is not permitted to act.
Mrs Boffin's love is real. But the old man — old Harmon — calls, and the child must go.
Property overrides tenderness. Every time, in this novel, property wins the first round.
And when I think about what the novel leaves unsettled, I think about Charley Hexam.
Here is a boy who climbed exactly as the system said he should — through education, through respectability, through alliance with a man of standing.
And his reward is to be used and discarded by Bradley Headstone.
Charley turns on Headstone with this extraordinary accusation — listen to how cold it is:
Not a word about his sister. Not a word about the violence. Only: you forgot to think about me.
Dickens doesn't redeem Charley. He lets that moral emptiness stand.
Daniel is right that Charley is one of the novel's most uncomfortable portraits, and Dickens knows exactly what he's doing there.
The ideology of self-improvement promised that merit would be recognised, that a man who worked hard and kept clean hands would rise.
Charley believed it. It hollowed him out.
But I keep returning to the other end of the social scale — to Twemlow.
The novel opens with this gorgeous, appalling joke about a man reduced to a piece of furniture.
Dickens writes — and I find this one of the funniest and bleakest sentences in all the novel:
The further he's pulled out — the more socially useful he becomes — the further he is from the centre of things.
That is Dickens's model of how society works, laid out as farce, in the first twenty pages.
And yet Twemlow gets the last word in the novel — literally.
The dining-table finally speaks. The furniture refuses to be furniture.
That is one of the things I treasure most about this novel — that the characters Dickens seems to set up as comic objects eventually claim their humanity.
Although not all of them. Not Charley.
What I find most searching — most radical — is the passage James didn't get to, the train crossing the river.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary image of industrial modernity obliterating everything in its path.
Here is the sentence — and it is worth every word:
A bomb-shell. That is what Dickens thinks industrial capitalism is doing to the city.
The river is still there beneath it. The dust-heaps are still there. But the force tearing through them has no interest in what it destroys.
And the train goes straight to its end — Dickens says — as Father Time goes to his.
That is not a redemption. That is a warning.
The train passage is also, historically, precise in a way that rewards attention.
The ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for the railway — that was the literal reality of Victorian railway building in London.
Working-class neighbourhoods demolished without compensation, the displaced simply pushed elsewhere.
Dickens embeds that history in a sentence of such velocity that you almost miss what it's saying.
The novel does that again and again — smuggles the unbearable inside the exhilarating.
Smuggles the unbearable inside the exhilarating — I think that might be the best single description of Dickens's method I've heard.
We've moved today from the dust and money at the heart of the novel, through its battered characters and ferocious institutions, to this final image: a train, a river, a warning.
My thanks to Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who have helped us see this novel's full and difficult weight.
Our Mutual Friend does not offer easy comfort. It offers something rarer: honesty about the world that made it.
Thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.

c41:p7.text:
In those pleasant little towns on Thames, you may hear the fall of the
      water over the weirs, or even, in still weather, the rustle of the rushes;
      and from the bridge you may see the young river, dimpled like a young
      child, playfully gliding away among the trees, unpolluted by the
      defilements that lie in wait for it on its course, and as yet out of
      hearing of the deep summons of the sea. It were too much to pretend that
      Betty Higden made out such thoughts; no; but she heard the tender river
      whispering to many like herself, ‘Come to me, come to me! When the cruel
      shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me! I
      am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I
      am not held in estimation according as I shirk it. My breast is softer
      than the pauper-nurse’s; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the
      pauper-wards. Come to me!’

c46:p56.text:
The confiding young man besought him to state his case. The innocent
      Twemlow, expecting Fledgeby to be astounded by what he should unfold, and
      not for an instant conceiving the possibility of its happening every day,
      but treating of it as a terrible phenomenon occurring in the course of
      ages, related how that he had had a deceased friend, a married civil
      officer with a family, who had wanted money for change of place or change
      of post, and how he, Twemlow, had ‘given him his name,’ with the usual,
      but in the eyes of Twemlow almost incredible result that he had been left
      to repay what he had never had. How, in the course of years, he had
      reduced the principal by trifling sums, ‘having,’ said Twemlow, ‘always to
      observe great economy, being in the enjoyment of a fixed income limited in
      extent, and that depending on the munificence of a certain nobleman,’ and
      had always pinched the full interest out of himself with punctual pinches.
      How he had come, in course of time, to look upon this one only debt of his
      life as a regular quarterly drawback, and no worse, when ‘his name’ had
      some way fallen into the possession of Mr Riah, who had sent him notice to
      redeem it by paying up in full, in one plump sum, or take tremendous
      consequences. This, with hazy remembrances of how he had been carried to
      some office to ‘confess judgment’ (as he recollected the phrase), and how
      he had been carried to another office where his life was assured for
      somebody not wholly unconnected with the sherry trade whom he remembered
      by the remarkable circumstance that he had a Straduarius violin to dispose
      of, and also a Madonna, formed the sum and substance of Mr Twemlow’s
      narrative. Through which stalked the shadow of the awful Snigsworth, eyed
      afar off by money-lenders as Security in the Mist, and menacing Twemlow
      with his baronial truncheon.

‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.

‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our

‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should

‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

c63:p48.text:
‘John dear,’ said Bella, ‘you’re a good nurse; will you please hold baby?’
      Having deposited the Inexhaustible in his arms with those words, Bella
      looked hard at Mr Boffin, who had moved to a table where he was leaning
      his head upon his hand with his face turned away, and, quietly settling
      herself on her knees at his side, and drawing one arm over his shoulder,
      said: ‘Please I beg your pardon, and I made a small mistake of a word when
      I took leave of you last. Please I think you are better (not worse) than
      Hopkins, better (not worse) than Dancer, better (not worse) than
      Blackberry Jones, better (not worse) than any of them! Please something
      more!’ cried Bella, with an exultant ringing laugh as she struggled with
      him and forced him to turn his delighted face to hers. ‘Please I have
      found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don’t believe you are a
      hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don’t believe you ever for one
      single minute were!’
c63:p48.summary: Bella, having placed the baby in John's arms, kneels beside Mr Boffin and experiences a profound revelation: she retracts her earlier contemptuous words and declares her new understanding that he is essentially good, having designed his harsh performance to correct her character.

c9:p28.text:
‘Yes; and it’s pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin,’ said her
      husband, ‘and it’s been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a
      year!’ It was ruin to Mrs Boffin’s aspirations, but, having so spoken,
      they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
